title: Research and publications
text:
Peer-reviewed publication
Problem. Alzheimer’s disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) are easiest to treat when caught early, but MRI-based deep-learning classifiers struggle with the task: the stages look alike on a scan, labelled data is scarce, and convolutional networks overfit easily.
What we did. We trained convolutional neural networks to classify brain MRI scans into four stages (non-demented, very mild, mild and moderate dementia) on the Kaggle Augmented Alzheimer dataset. Rather than proposing one fixed network, we optimised the architecture: eleven CNN variants were compared while tuning the learning rate, batch size, dropout rate and optimiser (Adam, AdamW, SGD) in an ablation study.
Result. The best configuration reached 90.6 % accuracy, 96 % specificity and a 90 % F1-score. The high specificity matters clinically: few healthy patients are wrongly flagged.
My contribution. The paper grew out of my Bachelor’s final-year project at Bahria University (see below), which I designed and implemented: the CNN pipeline, the optimiser ablation and the hyperparameter search.
Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease · Mild Cognitive Impairment · convolutional neural networks · deep learning · hyperparameter optimisation

title: Urban trees of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
text:
Introduction
Trees in a town are public infrastructure: they shade streets, absorb rainwater and shape the character of a neighbourhood, but they also age, get injured, and sometimes become a safety risk. To manage them, municipalities keep an inventory that records where each tree is, what it is, how big it is and what condition it is in.
This report explores the urban tree inventory of Saint-Germain-en-Laye (Yvelines, France), published as open data on data.gouv.fr. Each row is one tree, described by its location, species, dimensions, planting environment, a phytosanitary inspection (collar, trunk and crown) and an overall health diagnosis.
Objectives

title: Urban trees of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
text:
Understand the structure and quality of the data (types, missing values, duplicates, implausible values).
Describe each important variable: distributions, dominant categories and outliers.
Explore relationships between tree size, age, vigour and health.
Explore where the trees are, and where the unhealthy ones are.

title: Urban trees of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
text:
Data preparation
Raw open data is rarely analysis-ready. This section makes the following changes, each of which is explained in the code comments:

Standardise names and text. Column names become snake_case, extra spaces are trimmed, and empty strings become proper missing values (NA).
Decode the legend. Short codes are replaced by readable labels. Where the legend defines an order (e.g. age classes, health classes), the variable is stored as an ordered factor so plots and tables keep that order.
Convert units. Height is stored in centimetres in the source (a hauteur of 1000 is classed H2, “5 to 10 m”), so it is converted to metres.
Repair species names. The species field contains cultivar and author fragments (e.g. Europaea - - Pallida), so only the species epithet is kept and combined with the genus.
Flag implausible values. An impossible planting year is set to NA rather than silently kept.



Show code
# Step 1 - tidy names and text (kept as `trees_clean` so data-quality checks use the source values)
trees_clean <- trees_raw |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(str_squish(.x), "")))

# Helper: replace legend codes with labels; undocumented codes are kept as they are
decode <- function(x, map, ordered = FALSE) {
  x   <- as.character(x)
  lab <- unname(map[x])
  lab <- if_else(is.na(lab) & !is.na(x), x, lab)
  lev <- c(unname(map), setdiff(unique(lab), c(unname(map), NA)))
  droplevels(factor(lab, levels = lev, ordered = ordered))
}

# Step 2 - labels taken from the dataset legend (PDF)
lab_soil <- c(P = "Mulch", G = "Grass", S = "Stabilised", Gr = "Grate", GR = "Gravel",
              MA = "Planting bed", E = "Asphalt", CS = "Ground cover")
lab_age  <- c(J = "Young (<10 y)", JA = "Young adult (10-20 y)", A = "Adult (20-40 y)",
              AM = "Mature adult (50-70 y)")
lab_hgt  <- c(H1 = "0-5 m", H2 = "5-10 m", H3 = "10-15 m", H4 = "15-20 m", H5 = "20-25 m")
lab_circ <- c(C1 = "0-0.5 m", C2 = "0.5-1 m", C3 = "1-1.5 m", C4 = "1.5-2 m", C5 = "2-2.5 m",
              C6 = "2.5-3 m", C7 = "3-3.5 m")
lab_hab  <- c(L = "Free", SL = "Semi-free", R5 = "Screen (5 faces)", RR = "Reduced-relaxed",
              A = "Architectural")
lab_vig  <- c(D = "Declining", PP = "Low growth", MP = "Medium growth", P = "Growing")
lab_life <- c(`4` = "< 5 years", `3` = "5-10 years", `2` = "10-15 years", `1` = "> 15 years")
lab_diag <- c(C1 = "C1 Healthy", C2 = "C2 Minor lesions", C3 = "C3 Major lesions",
              C4 = "C4 Major, worsening", C5 = "C5 Removal needed")
lab_sit  <- c(Alignement = "Street row", Isolé = "Isolated", Groupe = "Group", Bosquet = "Grove")

trees <- trees_clean |>
  mutate(
    # categorical variables
    soil          = decode(type_sol, lab_soil),
    age_class     = decode(classe_age, lab_age, ordered = TRUE),
    height_class  = decode(classe_hauteur, lab_hgt, ordered = TRUE),
    circ_class    = decode(classe_circonference, lab_circ, ordered = TRUE),
    habit         = decode(port_arbre, lab_hab),
    vigour        = decode(vigueur_pousse, lab_vig, ordered = TRUE),
    life_expect   = decode(esperance_maintien, lab_life, ordered = TRUE),
    diagnostic    = decode(classification_diagnostic, lab_diag, ordered = TRUE),
    situation_lbl = decode(situation, lab_sit),
    district      = str_replace(quartier, "^Quartier (\\d+) - ", "Q\\1 - "),
    # taxonomy: genus + species epithet only
    genus         = genre_arbre,
    species       = if_else(is.na(genre_arbre) | is.na(espece_arbre), NA_character_,
                            paste(genre_arbre, str_to_lower(word(espece_arbre, 1)))),
    # numeric variables
    height_m          = hauteur / 100,
    circumference_cm  = circonference_en_cm,
    plantation_year   = if_else(date_plantation >= 1800, date_plantation, NA_real_),
    permeable_surface = surf_permeable
  )

num_labels <- c(height_m = "Height (m)",
                circumference_cm = "Circumference (cm)",
                plantation_year = "Planting year",
                permeable_surface = "Permeable surface")
num_vars <- names(num_labels)

diag_cols <- setNames(c("#2a9d8f", "#8ab17d", "#e9c46a", "#f4a261", "#e76f51"),
                      levels(trees$diagnostic))


The cleaned table trees keeps every original variable and adds the readable ones. From here on, the analysis focuses on four numeric variables (height, circumference, planting year and permeable surface) and a set of categorical variables (age class, habit, vigour, soil, situation, diagnosis…).

Two problems appear in Table 4.5. First, a single tree has a planting year of 200, which is not possible, so it is excluded from anything involving planting year. Height, circumference and permeable surface are all right-skewed (Figure 4.3): most trees are small or medium-sized and a few are very large. Planting years pile up on a few rounded values (1980, 2000, 2010) rather than spreading smoothly over time.

Outliers
Outliers are flagged with the standard IQR rule: a value is an outlier if it lies more than 1.5 x IQR below the first quartile or above the third quartile.


Show code

  group_by(Variable = variable) |>
  summarise(
    `Lower bound` = quantile(value, .25) - 1.5 * IQR(value),
    `Upper bound` = quantile(value, .75) + 1.5 * IQR(value),
    Outliers      = sum(value < `Lower bound` | value > `Upper bound`),
    `Share (%)`   = round(100 * Outliers / n(), 1),
    .groups = "drop"

The outliers in Table 4.7 are mostly genuine: old, large trees and wide planting beds exist in any town. They are therefore kept rather than removed. The one truly erroneous value (planting year 200) was already handled in Data quality.



Categorical variables
Categorical variables describe the tree itself (age class, size class, crown habit), its surroundings (soil, situation) and its condition (vigour, diagnosis). Bars are shown with counts and percentages, in the natural order of the legend when there is one.


Show code
var_labels <- c(age_class = "Age class", height_class = "Height class",
                circ_class = "Circumference class", habit = "Crown habit",
                soil = "Soil at tree foot", situation_lbl = "Situation",
                diagnostic = "Diagnosis", vigour = "Growth vigour",
                life_expect = "Expected remaining lifespan")

# Several categorical variables as small-multiple bar charts
facet_bars <- function(df, vars, ncol = 2) {
  counts <- map_dfr(vars, \(v) {
    d <- df |> filter(!is.na(.data[[v]])) |> count(level = .data[[v]])
    if (!is.ordered(df[[v]])) d <- arrange(d, desc(n))
    d |> mutate(variable = v, level = as.character(level),
                pct = n / sum(n), label = paste0(n, " (", percent(pct, accuracy = 1), ")"))
  }) |>
    mutate(key = paste(variable, level, sep = "___"))

  counts |>
    mutate(key = factor(key, levels = rev(unique(key))),
           variable = factor(variable, levels = vars, labels = var_labels[vars])) |>
    ggplot(aes(n, key)) +
    geom_col(fill = main_col) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .35))) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) str_remove(x, "^.*___")) +
    facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = ncol) +
    labs(x = "Number of trees", y = NULL)
}

# One variable, top-n levels
plot_cat <- function(df, var, n = 15, xlab = "Number of trees") {
  df |>
    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]])) |>
    count(level = as.character(.data[[var]]), sort = TRUE) |>
    slice_head(n = n) |>
    mutate(label = paste0(n, " (", percent(n / sum(!is.na(df[[var]])), accuracy = 1), ")")) |>
    ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(str_wrap(level, 30), n))) +
    geom_col(fill = main_col) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .2))) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL)
}



Structure of the tree population


Show code
facet_bars(trees, c("age_class", "height_class", "circ_class", "habit", "soil", "situation_lbl"))








Figure 4.5: Age, size, habit, soil and situation of the trees (count and share of trees with a known value).





The population is dominated by adult and young-adult trees on street rows, mostly under 10 m tall (Figure 4.5). Very old trees (mature adults) and isolated or grove trees are rare, so conclusions about them rest on very few observations.


Health and vigour


Show code

  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8))








Figure 4.6: Health diagnosis, growth vigour and expected remaining lifespan.





Most trees are in good condition (Figure 4.6): they are classed C1 or C2, grow vigorously and are expected to live more than 15 more years. Trees needing removal (C5) and declining trees are a small minority, but they matter most to the municipality.


Neighbourhoods


Show code

Figure 4.7: Number of inventoried trees per neighbourhood.








Species and genus
A single genus can dominate a town’s canopy, which makes it vulnerable to one pest or disease. The next two figures show how concentrated the inventory is.


Show code

Figure 4.8: The 10 most frequent tree genera.







Show code

Figure 4.9: The 15 most frequent species (genus + species epithet; cultivars are merged).





The canopy is highly concentrated (Figure 4.8 and Figure 4.9): the most frequent genus alone represents 49% of the trees, and the 26 genera in total are unevenly represented.


Planting dates


Show code

  filter(!is.na(plantation_year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(plantation_year)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = main_col, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Planting year", y = "Number of trees")








Figure 4.10: Number of trees by planting year (5-year bins).





Figure 4.10 shows the age structure of the town’s trees. Planting years are usually rounded to a decade in the source (1980, 1990, 2000…), so the spikes are partly an artefact of estimation and should not be read as precise planting campaigns. The health diagnoses themselves were all made in 2020.

title: Urban trees of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
text:
Bivariate analysis
Having described the variables one at a time, we now ask how they relate to each other: does bigger mean older, and does age or size go with poorer health?

Correlations between numeric variables
Because the distributions are skewed, Spearman rank correlation is used: it measures whether two variables increase together without assuming a straight-line relationship.


Show code
cor_mat <- trees |>
  select(all_of(num_vars)) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
dimnames(cor_mat) <- list(num_labels, num_labels)

cor_mat |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(var1 = factor(var1, levels = num_labels), var2 = factor(var2, levels = rev(num_labels))) |>
  ggplot(aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b2182b", mid = "white", high = "#2166ac", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Spearman r") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))








Figure 4.11: Spearman rank correlations between the numeric variables.





Height and circumference are strongly and positively linked (Figure 4.11), as expected for a growing tree, and both are negatively linked to planting year: older trees are taller and thicker. Circumference is very strongly tied to planting year, height only moderately. Permeable surface has a weaker link with size (around 0.3).


Show code
ggplot(trees, aes(circumference_cm, height_m)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = age_class), width = 1.5, height = .15, alpha = .5, size = 1.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = .7, formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = .9, na.value = "grey70") +
  labs(x = "Circumference (cm)", y = "Height (m)", colour = "Age class")








Figure 4.12: Height against circumference, coloured by age class, with a smoothed trend (loess). Points are slightly jittered because heights and circumferences are recorded in rounded steps.







Size by category


Show code
trees |>
  filter(!is.na(age_class)) |>
  ggplot(aes(age_class, circumference_cm)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = main_col, alpha = .6, outlier.alpha = .3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Circumference (cm)")








Figure 4.13: Circumference by age class.





The age classes in the data line up with the measurements (Figure 4.13): circumference rises steadily from “young” to “mature adult”. This reassures us that the age classes are consistent with the measured dimensions.


Show code
top_genera <- trees |> count(genus, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 6) |> pull(genus)

trees |>
  filter(genus %in% top_genera) |>
  mutate(genus = fct_reorder(genus, height_m, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(genus, height_m)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = main_col, alpha = .6, outlier.alpha = .3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Height (m)")








Figure 4.14: Height of the six most frequent genera (sorted by median).





Typical heights are similar across the main genera, with medians of roughly 5 to 7 m (Figure 4.14). Genus therefore explains little of the variation in height on its own; individual tree age and growing conditions matter more.


Health, age and vigour
Do older trees tend to be in worse condition, and does the diagnosis match the observed growth vigour? Each column of the heatmaps is scaled to 100 %, so cells compare shares within a group, and the printed number is the tree count.


Show code
plot_heat <- function(df, x, y, xlab, ylab) {
  df |>
    drop_na(all_of(c(x, y))) |>
    count(xv = .data[[x]], yv = .data[[y]]) |>
    group_by(xv) |>
    mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(xv, yv, fill = share)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = n, colour = share > .55), size = 3.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "black")) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f2f9f8", high = "#1b6f66", labels = percent) +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = ylab, fill = "Share\nwithin column") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))
}




Show code
plot_heat(trees, "age_class", "diagnostic", "Age class", "Diagnosis")








Figure 4.15: Health diagnosis by age class (label = number of trees; colour = share within each age class).







Show code
plot_heat(trees, "vigour", "diagnostic", "Growth vigour", "Diagnosis")








Figure 4.16: Health diagnosis by growth vigour (label = number of trees; colour = share within each vigour class).





Two patterns stand out. Older trees are more often diagnosed with lesions than young ones: the share of healthy (C1) trees falls steadily from young to adult trees (Figure 4.15). The few declining trees are mostly in the worst classes (Figure 4.16), but the link is not a clean gradient: trees with low growth are often classed C1, possibly because many are young trees that have not yet reached full vigour. Several cells contain only a handful of trees, so percentages there should be read with caution.

title: Urban trees of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
text:
Key findings

Data quality: the inventory is clean and complete where it matters. There are no duplicates. Missing values are concentrated in optional comments and planned-work columns. Two issues were found and handled: an impossible planting year (200) and a diametre column that is exactly twice circumference / pi in every row.
Dominant species / genera: the canopy is concentrated. Tilia alone makes up 49% of the 709 trees, and the three most frequent genera together make up 69%.
Size and age structure: the population is mostly adult and young-adult trees, planted mostly since 1980. Height and circumference are strongly correlated, older trees are larger, and the age classes agree with the measurements.
Health status: 91% of the assessed trees are healthy or have only minor lesions (C1-C2), and 73% are expected to live more than 15 more years. 10 trees are classed C5 (removal needed) and 5 are declining. Lesions become more frequent with age, although very old trees are too few to draw firm conclusions.
Spatial pattern: 93% of the trees stand in street rows, so the map follows the road network. The neighbourhood with the most trees is Q2 - Alsace - Pereire (296 trees).

title: Urban trees of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
text:
Limitations and next steps
Limitations

The inventory is a snapshot: all diagnoses were made in 2020, so it says nothing about how condition changes over time.
Several classes have very few trees (mature adults, isolated trees, C4-C5), so comparisons involving them are fragile.
Planting years are rounded (estimated) and the legend leaves a gap between the “adult” (20-40 y) and “mature adult” (50-70 y) classes.
The diametre column is unreliable and the unit of surf_permeable is not documented in the legend.
A few codes appear in the data but are not in the legend (for example soil type TV); they are kept as-is.
Coordinates are rounded to three decimals, which limits the spatial precision.

Possible next steps

Group rare categories into “Other” before any modelling.
Predict the health diagnosis or expected lifespan from age, size, genus and planting environment, keeping in mind the class imbalance.
Link tree density and health to streets or land use, and compare with a later inventory to measure change.

title: Late again? What’s really behind TGV delays
text:
Data
The original project is an interactive Bokeh server app that works as the slide deck of our talk: a hook, a map of the rail network, then four acts that follow Shneiderman’s mantra, overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand (Shneiderman 1996). This chapter tells the same story for the portfolio. The figures below are re-drawn in R from the same SNCF files, downloaded by code at render time, so every number in the text is recomputed rather than copied from the report.
SNCF publishes three monthly punctuality files on data.gouv.fr. Each level of the story uses its own file: the national rate is not the average of axes or routes, because one train can belong to several routes but counts only once nationally.
Show code
sncf_url <- "https://ressources.data.sncf.com/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/%s/exports/csv?use_labels=true"
tgv_files <- c(national = "reglarite-mensuelle-tgv-nationale",   # (sic: SNCF's file name)
               axes     = "regularite-mensuelle-tgv-axes",
               routes   = "regularite-mensuelle-tgv-aqst")

dir.create(here("data", "raw"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
tgv_path <- \(key) here("data", "raw", paste0(tgv_files[[key]], ".csv"))
for (key in names(tgv_files)) {
  if (!file.exists(tgv_path(key)))
    download.file(sprintf(sncf_url, tgv_files[[key]]), tgv_path(key), mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
}

read_sncf <- \(key) read_delim(tgv_path(key), delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE)

title: Late again? What’s really behind TGV delays
text:
File
Level
Used for




reglarite-mensuelle-tgv-nationale
all TGVs, monthly, from 2015
Act 1: the big picture


regularite-mensuelle-tgv-axes
per axis (Nord, Est, Atlantique, Sud-Est, Europe, OUIGO)
Act 2: regions


regularite-mensuelle-tgv-aqst
per route, with train counts and six delay causes, from 2018
Acts 3 and 4





Cleaning decisions
The full log of ambiguities and decisions lives in the project’s DATA_NOTES.md. The ones that matter for this chapter:

% late is computed from counts: late trains ÷ (planned − cancelled). Yearly and group figures sum the counts first, then divide, never averaging percentages.
Months with zero planned trains are dropped (nothing to measure).
Rows whose six cause shares are all zero keep their counts but are left out of the cause analysis.
Cause shares are weighted by each row’s number of late trains, so a 3-train route does not weigh as much as a 300-train one.
Causes are compared on full years 2018–2025: the categories appear to change around May 2026.

Act 3 · It’s where, not how far
In the app, a route map and a duration-versus-delay scatter share one data source, so selecting routes on either highlights them on both. The first hypothesis, long routes are late more often, did not hold: trip duration barely relates to the share late. What does matter is where a route runs.

One accent colour per chart: grey for context, vermillion for the series the story follows.

Monthly totals, not individual trains.
Delay causes are self-reported by SNCF; the categories seem to change in 2026 and the passenger share jumps suddenly in January 2021.

title: Agentic AI for predictive maintenance
text:
The question
An aircraft engine is monitored flight after flight. At a given flight t, an engineer asks:
Three situations are possible: gradual ageing (normal), compressor fouling (needs an engine inspection) and sensor drift (needs a sensor check, not an engine inspection). The task is to build an agent: a language model that reads the documentation, decides which diagnostic tools to call, and writes a justified recommendation. It must be able to say “insufficient information” and must never treat a tool’s output as a definitive diagnosis.
crumbs: 6  Agentic AI for predictive maintenance

title: Agentic AI for predictive maintenance
text: Based on the information available up to flight t, is there evidence of a concerning trend? What are the plausible causes, and what check should be recommended?
crumbs: 6  Agentic AI for predictive maintenance

title: Agentic AI for predictive maintenance
text:
What I built


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
            theme(plot.title.position = "plot",
                  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                  legend.position = "top"))

phm_dir <- here("data", "safran")


1. A rule-based baseline without an LLM. Alert when the exhaust-gas temperature margin (1150 K minus the LPT inlet temperature) stays below a threshold for p consecutive usable flights. The persistence rule avoids alerting on one noisy flight. The supervisors suggested a threshold of 11.5 K; I swept threshold and persistence over a grid on the development trajectories, then evaluated the chosen setting once on held-out test trajectories.
2. A single tool-using agent (LangChain + Ollama, temperature 0) with four tools bound to one engine and cut at the decision time, so the model physically cannot look into the future:







Tool
What it returns




lire_observations(debut, fin)
sensor readings and flight conditions, ≤ 30 flights per call


estimer_sante(debut, fin)
six health indicators estimated by a pretrained inverse MLP


calculer_marge(debut, fin)
the thermal (EGT) margin per flight


regle_seuil_marge()
(optional) the baseline rule’s verdict, as one more piece of evidence



The agent receives the knowledge base as its system prompt and must answer with one of five actions: continue monitoring, intensify monitoring, request an engine inspection, request a sensor check, or request additional data.
3. A fair evaluation harness. Every model gets the same tools, documents, prompt, decision time and step limit. Each run records the recommendation, the number of tool calls, the duration and the full reasoning trace (JSON lines). The expected action is derived from the hidden scenario labels by the evaluator only; the agent never sees them.

What the first runs show (Figure 6.2, Table 6.2):

Plumbing matters first. In run 1, most models produced no usable answer. Reading the traces showed why: models asked for flights after the decision time, the tool raised an exception, and the run died. Returning tool errors to the model as text (“window outside the authorised history, correct the arguments”) let it recover; in run 2, qwen3:8b answered every case.
The agent is cautious where the baseline is blind. On both sensor-drift engines, qwen3:8b recommended intensify monitoring (acceptable) where the baseline said “all fine”. But it also missed both fouling cases, while the baseline caught one.
Cost. About 15 tool calls and four to five minutes per case with a local model, against an instant rule.

So far, the agent is not better than a tuned rule on raw accuracy. The next question is whether it adds value on top of the rule.

title: Agentic AI for predictive maintenance
text:
Next steps

Give the agent the baseline rule as a tool (already implemented, flag --with-baseline-tool) and measure whether it combines the rule’s fouling detection with its own caution on drift.
Add trend and change-point tools, so the model does not have to spot a slow drift by reading 30-row tables.
Evaluate on more engines and several decision times, and score the justification (evidence cited, alternatives considered), not just the final action.
